speechtext:
With regard to the ques-
'Mr. Gobeil.l
tion asked the other day by the right hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) regarding political meetings in camps, I might say that in October last year, at the time of the provincial election, in British Columbia a regulation was established that there should be no political meetings held in the camps. To the best of my knowledge no complaints were received from any party with regard to that regulation. When the provincial election in Ontario was called the same regulation was in effect and letters were sent out to the superintendents at the camps so stating. Now the situation in Ontario is that the provincial government also have camps, and I find on inquiry that they have not any similar regulation; they permit meetings in the camps. Under these circumstances it has been thought wise to withdraw the regulation that was issued by our department and to permit the same state of affairs to exist as prevails in the provincial camps, so that meetings will be allowed. The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Heenan) came to the department on Saturday to present the case and he was assured that he would be given every courtesy at any camp that he might desire to visit.

May I ask the Secretary of State whether he intends to propose any amendments to this bill? We were led to believe by the fine speeches that were delivered by some of the ministers and supporters of the government that amendments were to be introduced. Is that the intention?

I was not aware that any
suggestion had been made to the minister that amendments to this bill should be made on his motion. The bill passed the house by a majority of fifty-seven and was referred to a select committee. That select committee has reported the bill as it stands.

On this point, may I say
that the vote was taken with the understanding that we could make proper amendments to the bill? I was asked by my leader to sit on that committee which was composed of seven members. The senior member for Ottawa (Mr. Chevrier) and I were the two Liberal members; the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Maclnnis) represented the independent parties in the house, and there were four Conservative members. What the senior member for Ottawa and I did in this matter was to try to get the best available information about the translation business.

May I interrupt the hon.

I have much respect for
the Secretary of State and he knows this more than anyone else.

I have great compassion
for those who live under the same roof as the hon. member for North Huron (Mr. Spotton) because if he snores as loudly as he breathes, no one could sleep where he was.
I was saying that I have much respect for the Secretary of State and I admit that he came to the committee to make a statement; that he made it and that afterwards, as he says, he left. While he was still in the committee room I said: " Please stay here because I have questions to ask you." Nevertheless he left. I said this in an audible voice.

I am not a member of the

What I said to the hon. gentleman was that I wanted to ask him for some information as a member of a committee appointed by this house, and what is forgotten now is that the committee on the civil service, of which we were members, was not a committee of the government, which is itself a committee of the house, but was a committee of the house; and to that committee the hon. gentleman (Mr. Cahan) came as the

Well, I am relating what happened, and what the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George has just said confirms exactly and absolutely what I said before. Is there some barking? My hon. friend from Restigouche-Madawaska (Mr. Michaud), with whom I fought the last campaign, said we were going to the dogs; well, I hope the bill will have the same fate. When I mentioned in that committee the fact that two years ago one of the recommendations of the committee was to superannuate the three civil service commissioners I wondered how it happened that the chairman of the commission, whose superannuation had been recommended by the committee, is still enjoying his job. I did not understand why the government had not complied with that recommendation of the committee. One reason for that recommendation of the committee two years ago was that the chairman of the civil service commission was too old to sit there. Two years have elapsed and yet he keeps his job, while two others have been superannuated. Also as a French Canadian and a French speaking member of this house I felt it very much that although one of the civil service commissioners is French speaking an order was passed by the commission that the commissioner who should come before the committee to give evidence about translation was not the French speaking civil service commissioner, who was supposed to have had some experience in translation, but another gentleman. For him I have great respect; he has shown great ability while giving evidence in the committee; it is my duty to give praise to whom praise is due. Nevertheless as a French speaking member of this house I resent very much the fact that the civil service commission decided that the man who was to give evidence on translation was not bilingual, while another civil service commissioner was. I regard it as an outrage on the French speaking members of this house. I submit this dilemma to the Secretary of State, who has the responsibility of reporting to the house about the civil service commission; either Mr. Potvin, the French speaking and bilingual civil service commissioner who has been a translat-"or", as the chairman of the committee would say, and was a distinguished civil ser-"vant", as the chairman would say, is competent or he is not. If he is competent, the civil service commission has no excuse whatever for not sending him to the committee to give explanations about the matter of translations; if he is incompetent, the government have no excuse for having appointed him to such a high post. I say now that when I was asked dn the Senate committee to make a statement with regard to the matter they had in hand, namely the cost of Senate translation, I said what I had said in the House of Commons. Now it was ascertained by one of the committee under the control of the treasury that the setting up in type of these corrections made in the text after it had been set up in type and sent for revision-not all French, but a' great deal of it, some of it being in English -over a series of years, in wages in respect of the resetting of that type, after it had been first set up in the printer's text, varied in cost from $75,000 to $80,000 a year during a number of . years preceding 1933; and in the first ten months of 1933 the setting up of such changes as those I have mentioned cost $52,000.

The original in English is first sent to the printer, and the printer puts it into type. After it is put into type the proof is taken off the galley. The galley proof is read by the expert proofreader in the printing bureau. It is then submitted in page form, or perhaps in galley form, to the author. Any errors which the author discovers and which have not been discovered by the printer are marked by him. If he chooses to change the original phraseology, he does so. I am referring not to the debates of the Senate or the House of Commons but to public reports and so on, laws printed in English and translated into French, or bills appearing before both houses of parliament. If the author sees fit
he may make changes in words or even sentences or whole paragraphs. It then goes back to the printer, who in turn makes the necessary changes as outlined in the author's list of changes. Let me point out here, sir, that in all the arguments which have been advanced touching upon the cost of authors' changes, or changes in faulty translation, not one word is to be found touching the cost of the changes made in the original English text. After that takes place the French translator is handed the printed matter from which he translates. Then it goes to the printer just the same as the English version. When it comes back to the translator and is looked over by him he corrects any faults he may discover. He may change the phraseology, a word here or a sentence or a paragraph. But what do I find peculiar in that? At the very moment a change is made it is photostated and held up as evidence to show that this extra cost is attributable in most part to faulty translation.
Let me give an example or two to show how it works. Everybody knows that the Canada Shipping Act was in bulk when it was submitted to the other chamber last session. That bill went before a committee of that chamber and it was changed by its author and by others who were not the authors but who made suggestions. The changes made in that bill were enormous. But before the bill went before the Senate committee in English it had been translated into French. When the bill was before the Senate committee it was found that in many respects it was unconstitutional, that clause after clause of the bill could not apply. The Senate therefore threw out most of that bill and left it over to this session when a new bill was framed and submitted to that chamber. But all these changes that were made in the English version in 1933 naturally brought about changes in the French translation, and those changes were all charged up to , faulty French translation. They were photostated, but no photostat was ever taken of the changes made in the English version of that bill.
This session I find that that bill is again before the Senate. There have been no less than two different editions of that bill this session. The first that was presented to the other chamber this session was so faulty in its construction in English that they had to call in new lawyers from British Columbia which cost two, three or four thousand dollars, and lawyers from Montreal, Ottawa, and elsewhere, in order to redraft the bill. After it was redrafted it was submitted in English and

Again they had to bring that bill down to something nearer perfection, and all the changes that were made in the English version in that bill necessitated similar changes in French. Yet I find that that is one of the items that is charged up to the extra cost of faulty French translation in the preparation of that bill. That very bill has been photostated and paraded about this country to show how faulty translation has taken place in the French translation of the documents and debates of this house.
Shame, shame.

I say, Mr. Chairman, that
that is unfair not only to the members of the translation staff but to the minister himself who is in charge of the printing bureau. It is most unfair that the impression should be created that the translators are either negligent or unfit for their duties. And to prove it they hold up a photostated copy of that bill extending to four or five hundred pages and say that that is a sample of the French translators' work, when as a matter of fact every change that was made in the French translation belongs to the category of authors' corrections in the English version, and not in the French.
They cannot answer that.
May I say to the hon. gentleman in regard to the photos I produced before the committee of the Senate that not a single change in French translation was due to a change in the original English.

But you took mighty good ;are not to produce any photostated English changes. The hon. gentleman cannot say that there were not numerous authors' changes. I can show them another Senate bill, letter B of the Senate, now before that house. I have a copy of it here. That bill has been changed in its English construction three different times since it was submitted to the Senate and every time a change was made in the English construction a change had to be made in the French translation, and every such change in the French translation was charged up to faulty translation.
Shame, shame.

Let me come a little nearer home. Take the marketing bill before this house. That bill contains twenty-one clauses and there have been from eighteen to twenty amendments. The bill was printed originally in English and then in French, and no fault
[Mr. Veniot.l
was found with the translation. The bill was then submitted to this house and certain amendments were suggested. The Minister of Agriculture withdrew the bill for a time in order to submit certain amendments, and as I say from eighteen to twenty amendments have been submitted in English and translated into French, and not a word of fault has been found with the translation of those amendments.
What do we find now? Some of the amendments have already been reamended, and when the bill comes again before the committee with all the changes that have been made in it we shall never know it for the original bill. All the changes that have thus been necessitated in the French translation of that bill, following it up until to-day with the eighteen or twenty amendments attached to it, will be charged to faulty translation, instead of placing the blame where it rightly belongs, on the Minister of Agriculture for not having the bill prepared in a proper way in the first place.
